foundations-0.transcript: What is nissology? The word was proposed in 1994 by the anthropologist Grant McCall, from the Greek nisos, meaning island. McCall defined it as the study of islands on their own terms. It grew out of a Pacific critique: aid agencies and mainland scholars tended to describe islands by what they lack: size, resources and connection. In the same year the Tongan writer Epeli Hau'ofa answered that story of smallness. He described Oceania not as scattered specks in an empty ocean, but as a sea of islands, connected by voyaging and kinship. Island studies then became a field with its own institutions: an international association in 1992, Island Studies Journal in 2006, and the island cultures journal Shima in 2007. Two ideas run through this whole course. First, islandness: isolation and boundedness shape what happens on islands, but they do not determine it. Always ask what the mechanism is. Second, whose terms? Most research on small islands is written by outsiders. That does not make it wrong, but it shapes which questions get asked. Your two foundation readings, by Godfrey Baldacchino and Adam Grydehøj, are essays about exactly these problems. Read them first: they are the lens for every case study that follows.

foundations-3.transcript: Why do some islands have many species and others very few? This is the question of island biogeography. Robert MacArthur and E. O. Wilson treated an island's species number as a balance of two rates. Immigration falls as the island fills up, because fewer new species are left to arrive. Extinction rises, because more species compete for the same space. Where the two curves cross, the number of species is stable. Watch what happens as the island gets bigger: extinction falls, and the equilibrium moves to the right. The theory explains a pattern seen on islands everywhere: the species–area relationship. On islands, a tenfold increase in area roughly doubles the number of species. The General Dynamic Model adds time. A volcanic island is born, grows in area and height, then erodes and sinks. Species richness and the number of unique, endemic species rise and then fall over the island's life. Surtsey, already shrinking only decades after its birth, is the fastest-moving test of this model. A third idea, the island rule, says that on islands small animals tend to evolve larger, and large animals smaller. Treat all three theories as models to test, not laws. Real islands get extra nutrients from seabirds, receive species carried by people, and sometimes were once joined to land.

foundations-4.transcript: Most of this course is spent reading research papers. Here is a method for reading them critically. Ask five questions of every paper. What is the single main claim? What method was used, where, when, and on what sample? Which figure or table carries the evidence, and does its arithmetic hold? What uncertainty is reported, and what is missing? And finally, scope: to which islands and conditions does the result really apply? The annotated papers use a colour code that matches these questions. Yellow marks the authors' argument. Green marks evidence. Blue marks method. Purple marks concepts to learn. Red means read critically. Orange links the paper to other units. Some papers cannot be shared openly, so for those you get a companion guide and a link to the publisher. After every video there is a short quiz. Get into the habit of answering before you look at the feedback.

funafuti-2.transcript: Are Tuvalu's islands shrinking? In 2018 Paul Kench and colleagues measured every one of the country's one hundred and one islands to find out. They compared aerial photographs from 1971 with satellite images from 2014. Over those four decades local sea level rose about fifteen centimetres, twice the global average. Yet Tuvalu's total land area grew by seventy-three and a half hectares, nearly three percent. Here is the change for each atoll, from the paper's Table 1. Eight of the nine atolls gained land. Funafuti gained about four percent. Now be a careful reader. Add up the hectare changes in Table 1 and you get about sixty-three hectares, not seventy-three and a half. And one percentage in the table looks wrong. Small inconsistencies like these are common. Your task is to work out whether they change the conclusion. Here they do not: most islands grew under every reading. The authors conclude that islands are dynamic features, not static landforms waiting to drown. But they are careful: under high-emission scenarios, the sea will rise much faster than in their study period, and the past may not be a guide.

falklands-0.transcript: The Falkland Islands: twelve thousand square kilometres of ancient rock in the cold South Atlantic. They lie about five hundred kilometres east of southern South America. Unlike every other island in this course, the Falklands are built of continental crust. The oldest rocks, in the far south of West Falkland, are about a billion years old. Above them lie hard quartzites and sandstones, and then sediments left by an ice age about three hundred million years ago. That sequence closely matches the rocks of South Africa. The leading explanation is that the Falklands block lay off south-eastern Africa within the supercontinent Gondwana, broke away as Gondwana split, and rotated about one hundred and eighty degrees on its way to its present position. Evidence from the magnetism of ancient rock supports a large rotation, though the details are still debated. Today the islands sit on a shallow continental plateau. Watch what happens when we lower the sea by one hundred and twenty-five metres, roughly the level of the last ice age.

falklands-3.transcript: When did people first reach the Falklands? The standard answer is 1690. New research suggests otherwise. In 2021 Kit Hamley and colleagues reported three lines of evidence from New Island: a sudden hundred-fold rise in charcoal in the peat, piles of sea lion and penguin bones dated to about thirteen hundred CE, and a stone spear point made of local quartzite. They suggest visits by seafaring people from Tierra del Fuego, centuries before Europeans. Fire matters here. Even today, fire is visible from orbit. In this photograph taken from the International Space Station, smoke streams from fires on East Falkland. The researchers argue that lightning-caused fires are rare in these islands, so a sudden surge of charcoal points to people. The colonial history is tangled. France and Britain both founded settlements in the 1760s. Spain bought out the French. After Spain left in 1811, Buenos Aires claimed the islands. Britain took control in 1833, the root of today's dispute. In 1982 Argentina invaded, and the war that followed cost about nine hundred lives.

tristan-0.transcript: Tristan da Cunha: the most remote inhabited island on Earth. It lies in the South Atlantic, about two thousand four hundred kilometres from St Helena and two thousand eight hundred from Cape Town. About one hundred and thirty-two million years ago, as Africa and South America began to separate, a plume of hot mantle erupted vast floods of lava in what are now Namibia and Brazil. As the Atlantic widened, the same plume built the Walvis Ridge. Tristan is the youngest island at the end of that track. The island is a single great cone rising to about two thousand and sixty metres. But most of the volcano is underwater: its flanks reach three thousand six hundred metres deep within twenty-five kilometres of the coast. Watch the sea drain away to reveal it. In 2020, Wolfram Geissler and colleagues published sonar maps of the seafloor around the islands. They found four hundred and thirty young volcanic cones, and two previously unknown seamounts. One of them, Isolde Seamount, was probably the source of a submarine eruption in 2004 that washed pumice onto Tristan's beaches.

tristan-3.transcript: From a passing navigator to a community of seven families. The Portuguese navigator Tristão da Cunha sighted the island in 1506. Britain garrisoned it in 1816, officially to stop it being used to rescue Napoleon from St Helena. When the soldiers left, Corporal William Glass and his family stayed. Women from St Helena joined in 1827, and two Italian sailors shipwrecked in 1892 added the names Repetto and Lavarello. On the tenth of October 1961, after weeks of earthquakes, a vent opened beside the village and built a dome of lava. The whole population was evacuated, first to Nightingale Island, then to England. They lived near Southampton for two years. Although they were offered permanent resettlement, most voted to go home, and returned in 1963. Journalists turned the return into a parable about modern life. The islanders' own accounts stress their land, their boats and their independence.

synthesis-0.transcript: Six islands, side by side. We have travelled from the central Pacific to the South Atlantic, the North Atlantic and the Arabian Sea. Their areas span four orders of magnitude, from Surtsey's one point three square kilometres to the Falklands' twelve thousand. Their ages span eight orders: from rocks a billion years old to land made in the 1960s. Notice that the inhabited islands are not necessarily the largest or most fertile. Access matters more: a landing place, a harbour, a lagoon. And so does history.

synthesis-1.transcript: How well did our theories do? Equilibrium theory fits Surtsey in outline, but seabirds moved the equilibrium. The General Dynamic Model describes Surtsey's shrinking and the Pitcairn chain, but not continental fragments. The island rule holds for gecko body size on Socotra, but not head shape. And Darwin's subsidence explains Funafuti, while Henderson shows the reverse: uplift. And the ethical question applies everywhere. In every case, the most-cited knowledge was produced by visiting scientists. Ask where islanders were: as authors, collaborators, or decision-makers.

synthesis-2.transcript: Your capstone: a profile of an island of your own choosing. Choose an island not covered in this course, ideally a lesser-known one. In three to four thousand words, explain its physical geography with a map or terrain figure, its ecology through theory, its history, and its culture and governance. Review at least four peer-reviewed papers using the five-question method. And finish with a reflection: whose terms does your own profile use? Need ideas? Try Kiritimati, Aldabra, Nauru, St Kilda, South Georgia, Rapa Iti, Lord Howe Island, Jan Mayen, or one of the many islands of Indonesia and the Philippines, which island studies has largely overlooked.
